hypothesis: Implementing a structured, minimally engineered integration pattern for AI-misinformation monitoring (via APIs and webhooks) into existing incident workflows will enable non-engineering leaders and their teams to achieve (a) faster, more reliable alert delivery into ticketing/chat systems and (b) clearer ownership handoffs to security and data science, compared with an ad-hoc, manual export-import approach.

baseline.description: Ad-hoc, manual handling of AI-misinformation monitoring signals where non-technical teams periodically export alerts from a monitoring tool (or receive them by email), manually triage them in spreadsheets, and copy-paste high-priority items into chat and ticketing tools.
implementation_outline: Monitoring tool (simulated via a Python script) writes JSON alert files to disk or emails a CSV export.
A non-technical operator (simulated script) reads the export once per fixed interval (e.g., every 10 minutes).
Operator filters alerts based on simple rules (e.g., severity >= 3, channel in ['twitter','tiktok']).
Operator posts selected alerts to a chat channel (simulated via stdout or a mock HTTP endpoint) and creates incident tickets by writing to a 'tickets' JSON log.
No automatic linkage between alerts and tickets; correlation is done manually using IDs in spreadsheets.
baseline.intended_learning: Characterize the friction, latency, and error risks when leaders rely on manual, non-integrated workflows for AI-misinformation alert handling.

treatment.description: Lightweight, script-based technical toolkit where AI-misinformation alerts are pushed via a webhook from a mock monitoring service into an integration layer that automatically routes them to a mock chat system and a mock incident/ticketing system, using a clear, human-readable configuration and non-technical specification.
implementation_outline: Mock monitoring service exposes an HTTP endpoint '/emit_alerts' that simulates AI-misinformation alerts and posts them to a webhook URL.

Integration service exposes '/webhook/alerts' that receives alerts, validates payloads against a documented schema, enriches them (e.g., maps to playbook type), and applies routing rules defined in a YAML or JSON config readable by non-engineers.
Integration service posts formatted alert summaries to a mock chat endpoint '/chat/post_message' and creates or updates incidents via '/tickets/create' and '/tickets/update'.

A simple, non-technical spec file (markdown) describes: inputs (alert fields), routing rules, SLAs, ownership, and failure behaviors; code is structured so non-engineers can adjust configurations without editing logic.
Logs and correlation IDs are automatically maintained across alerts, chat posts, and tickets, providing traceability for postmortems and pilots.
treatment.intended_learning: Demonstrate how a simple, well-specified integration pattern with APIs and webhooks can materially reduce latency, ambiguity, and coordination failure in AI-misinformation handling, while remaining understandable and governable by non-engineers.

workloads.name: workload-1-single-stream-medium-volume
workloads.description: Simulated steady stream of medium-volume AI-misinformation alerts (e.g., 100 alerts over 30 minutes) representing social content spikes about a brand, delivered first through the baseline pipeline and then through the treatment pipeline.
steps_baseline: Generate synthetic alerts and write them as JSON lines to 'data/baseline/alerts_stream.jsonl'.
Every 10 minutes, run a script that reads all new alerts since the last run.
Write filtered alerts to 'data/baseline/triage_sheet.csv' as a stand-in for a manual spreadsheet.
Simulate a human operator creating tickets and chat messages by running a script that reads 'triage_sheet.csv' and appends entries to 'logs/baseline_tickets.jsonl' and 'logs/baseline_chat.jsonl'.
Record timestamps for each stage to compute end-to-end latency and coverage.
steps_treatment: Start the mock chat, ticketing, and integration services.
Configure the monitoring simulator to POST each generated alert directly to the integration webhook '/webhook/alerts' as it is generated.
Integration service validates payloads, applies routing rules (e.g., severity >= 3 routed to both chat and tickets), and posts messages to '/chat/post_message' and '/tickets/create'.
All events are logged to 'logs/treatment_events.jsonl' with correlation IDs linking alert, chat post, and ticket.
Record timestamps at receipt, routing, and downstream delivery to compute end-to-end latency and coverage.

workloads.name: workload-2-multi-stream-incident-spike
workloads.description: Simulate a sudden spike of high-severity alerts across multiple channels (e.g., a deepfake executive video and coordinated narrative spread), testing how baseline and treatment workflows handle peak load and cross-team handoffs.
steps_baseline: Generate synthetic spike alerts and write them to 'data/baseline/spike_alerts.jsonl' over a compressed 5-minute timeline.
Simulate a manual export event triggered at minute 5.
Manual triage script filters alerts with severity_score >= 4 or scenario_tag in ['deepfake_executive_video', 'market_manipulation_rumor'] and writes them to 'data/baseline/spike_triage.csv'.

Simulate a human manually categorizing which team should own each item (e.g., comms, legal, security) using simplistic mapping rules in the script, and log results to 'logs/baseline_spike_team_assignments.jsonl'.
Simulate delayed ticket creation and chat posting with fixed manual delays (e.g., 5–15 minutes) added, then record final times and assignments.
steps_treatment: Start all mock services as in workload-1.
Monitoring simulator sends alerts in near real-time to integration webhook.

Integration layer uses configuration mapping (e.g., scenario_tag + severity_score) to automatically determine primary and secondary owning teams and routes alerts to team-specific chat channels and ticket queues.
Record times from first high-severity alert receipt to: first ticket created, first message in each relevant team channel, and first 'incident_opened' event in tickets.
Output correlation logs to 'logs/treatment_spike_events.jsonl' for analysis of routing accuracy and speed.

workloads.name: workload-3-failure-and-retry-scenarios
workloads.description: Evaluate resilience and observability differences between baseline and treatment when common integration failures occur (e.g., chat endpoint unavailable, ticketing API returns errors, malformed alert payloads).
steps_baseline: Generate synthetic alerts and a CSV export as usual.

Simulate operator attempting to paste alerts into a chat tool that is 'unavailable' (represented by the script dropping messages for 3 minutes and logging errors to 'logs/baseline_failures_chat.txt').
Simulate manual re-tries with a fixed probability (e.g., only 50% of failed posts are retried).
Simulate ticket creation failures as missed entries in 'logs/baseline_tickets.jsonl' due to lack of validation and unclear error reporting.
Manually count unrecovered failures and approximate detection of data quality issues (e.g., missing fields) by scanning the logs.
steps_treatment: Enable failure injection in mock chat and ticketing services according to the defined scenarios.
Run integration pipeline as in previous workloads.
Integration layer implements automatic retries with backoff, validation of incoming alerts, and error logging to 'logs/treatment_errors.jsonl'.
Measure fraction of alerts successfully delivered after retries, mean retry duration, and how many malformed alerts are rejected versus quarantined with error details.
Optionally, emit summary metrics to a simple console or JSON file for inspection.

controls.data_generation: Use the same synthetic alert generation scripts and random seeds for both baseline and treatment runs for each workload, ensuring identical input alert streams.
controls.environment: Run baseline and treatment on the same machine type and operating system, with the same Python version and library dependencies as specified in the repository (e.g., Python 3.11, identical requirements.txt).
controls.timing: For each workload, run baseline and treatment back-to-back under similar system load conditions. Do not run other heavy processes concurrently.
controls.configuration: Use a shared configuration file to define common concepts (severity thresholds, scenario tags, team names) so that logical routing rules are materially equivalent between baseline and treatment.
controls.logging_format: Standardize timestamps (ISO 8601 UTC), IDs, and field names across baseline and treatment logs to ensure comparability.
controls.run_order: Alternate starting condition across repeated trials (e.g., baseline-first on trial 1, treatment-first on trial 2) to mitigate any warm-cache or transient system effects if multiple iterations are run.

metrics.name: end_to_end_alert_to_ticket_latency
metrics.description: Time from initial detection timestamp of an alert to the creation timestamp of the corresponding incident/ticket entry.

metrics.name: end_to_end_alert_to_chat_latency
metrics.description: Time from initial detection timestamp of an alert to posting timestamp in the relevant chat channel.

metrics.name: alert_routing_coverage
metrics.description: Proportion of alerts that meet routing criteria (e.g., severity >= 3) and successfully appear as tickets and/or chat entries.

metrics.name: routing_accuracy
metrics.description: Proportion of routed alerts that are assigned to the correct owning team(s) according to a predefined ground-truth mapping derived from scenario tags and severity.

metrics.name: operator_touch_points
metrics.description: Estimated number of manual human interaction steps required to move an alert from detection to ticket creation and chat notification (e.g., export, copy-paste, manual classification). For this experiment, this is approximated by counting scripted manual-analog steps.

metrics.name: unrecovered_delivery_failures
metrics.description: Number of alerts that should have been routed but were not successfully delivered to chat or ticketing endpoints after all retries and manual efforts.

metrics.name: error_detection_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of malformed or incomplete alerts that are detected and logged as errors (with sufficient detail) versus silently dropped or misprocessed.

metrics.name: configuration_complexity
metrics.description: Relative complexity of integration logic expressed as the number of configuration lines (YAML/JSON) and distinct routing rules that non-engineers would need to understand or modify.

primary.description: For workloads 1 and 2, the median end_to_end_alert_to_ticket_latency and end_to_end_alert_to_chat_latency in the treatment should be at least 50% lower than in the baseline.

For workloads 1 and 2, the treatment should achieve alert_routing_coverage >= 0.95 and routing_accuracy >= 0.9 for alerts that meet routing criteria, and both metrics should be strictly higher than baseline.

secondary.description: In workload 3, the treatment should have at least 50% fewer unrecovered_delivery_failures compared with baseline, and an error_detection_rate >= 0.95 for deliberately malformed alerts.

Treatment should reduce operator_touch_points by at least 60% per 100 alerts compared with baseline while keeping configuration_complexity within a small, reviewable range (e.g., <= 150 config lines and <= 15 distinct routing rules).

success_criteria.interpretation_notes: Meeting primary criteria indicates that a simple, well-specified integration pattern is operationally superior to manual workflows for non-engineering-led AI-misinformation defense. Secondary criteria help assess sustainability and manageability for executives and cross-functional teams.

failure_modes.name: configuration_drift_or_misconfiguration
failure_modes.description: Non-engineers modify routing configurations (e.g., YAML rules) without sufficient validation, causing alerts to be misrouted or dropped.
mitigations: Provide schema validation and configuration checks in the integration service that fail fast with clear errors when config is invalid.
Include sample configuration files and change-control guidance in the repository, emphasizing non-technical spec review by technical partners.
Log configuration versions with each routed event for traceability.

failure_modes.name: clock_skew_and_timestamp_inconsistency
failure_modes.description: System clock differences between services lead to misleading latency measurements or misordered events.
mitigations: Normalize timestamps to UTC and use a single time source for synthetic generation and logging.
Document this requirement in setup instructions and provide a utility module for timestamp generation.

failure_modes.name: environment_dependency_issues
failure_modes.description: Inconsistent Python versions, missing dependencies, or port conflicts cause scripts or services to fail.
mitigations: Provide a requirements.txt and optional Dockerfile specifying versions.
Use environment variable defaults and clearly document configurable ports.
Offer a health-check script that verifies ability to bind to ports and import dependencies before running full workloads.

failure_modes.name: log_correlation_failures
failure_modes.description: Correlation IDs are not generated or propagated consistently, making it difficult to match alerts to tickets and chat messages for metric computation.
mitigations: Centralize correlation ID creation at the earliest point (alert generator) and pass it through all downstream systems.
Add automated tests in the repository to verify presence and consistency of correlation IDs across logs.

failure_modes.name: metric_computation_errors
failure_modes.description: Analysis notebooks misinterpret logs (e.g., wrong field names, time units) and compute incorrect latency or coverage values.
mitigations: Define a clear evidence_schema (see below) and ensure analysis scripts validate logs against it.
Include a small, known-good sample dataset with expected metric values for sanity checks.

required_environment.hardware: A standard laptop or workstation with at least 4 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, and 2 GB free disk space. No GPU required.

software.runtime: Python 3.10 or 3.11 (as specified in the repository)
software.dependencies: Installed via 'pip install -r requirements.txt' in the repository root.
software.optional: Docker (if using the containerized setup), Git for cloning the repository.

required_environment.network: Localhost-only operation by default. No internet access is required for core experiments; endpoints for chat/ticketing/monitoring are simulated as local HTTP services.

run_instructions:
Clone the repository:
  git clone https://github.com/bookauthority/defending-brand-trust-ai-misinformation.git
  cd defending-brand-trust-ai-misinformation

Set up a Python virtual environment (recommended) and install dependencies:
  python -m venv .venv
  source .venv/bin/activate  # on Windows: .venv\\Scripts\\activate
  pip install -r requirements.txt

Ensure required directories exist:
  mkdir -p data/baseline data/treatment logs config

Populate configuration files using provided templates (paths are examples; actual filenames should be aligned with the repo):
  - Copy 'config/templates/integration_rules.example.yaml' to 'config/integration_rules.yaml' and review routing rules.
  - Copy 'config/templates/teams.example.yaml' to 'config/teams.yaml' defining mock comms, legal, and security teams.
  - No code changes should be necessary for non-technical users; only configuration review and edits.

Run Workload 1 (baseline):
  - Generate synthetic alerts:
    python scripts/integrations/gen_alerts.py \
      --output data/baseline/alerts_stream.jsonl \
      --count 100 --duration-minutes 30 --seed 42
  - Run manual export and triage simulation:
    python scripts/integrations/baseline_manual_triage.py \
      --input data/baseline/alerts_stream.jsonl \
      --triage-output data/baseline/triage_sheet.csv
  - Simulate manual ticket and chat creation:
    python scripts/integrations/baseline_create_tickets_and_chat.py \
      --triage-input data/baseline/triage_sheet.csv \
      --tickets-log logs/baseline_tickets.jsonl \
      --chat-log logs/baseline_chat.jsonl

Run Workload 1 (treatment):
  - Start mock services in separate terminals or via a supervisor script:
    python scripts/integrations/mock_chat_service.py --port 8101
    python scripts/integrations/mock_ticketing_service.py --port 8102
    python scripts/integrations/integration_service.py \
      --port 8100 \
      --chat-url http://localhost:8101/chat/post_message \
      --ticket-url http://localhost:8102/tickets
  - Generate and emit alerts directly to the integration webhook:
    python scripts/integrations/gen_alerts.py \
      --output data/treatment/alerts_stream.jsonl \
      --count 100 --duration-minutes 30 --seed 42 \
      --webhook-url http://localhost:8100/webhook/alerts
  - Confirm that integration logs were written:
    ls logs/treatment_events.jsonl

Run Workload 2 (baseline and treatment) using analogous commands with different arguments, for example:
  - Baseline spike generation:
    python scripts/integrations/gen_alerts.py \
      --output data/baseline/spike_alerts.jsonl \
      --count 60 --duration-minutes 5 --seed 123 \
      --scenario spike
  - Baseline spike triage and routing simulation:
    python scripts/integrations/baseline_spike_triage_and_assign.py \
      --input data/baseline/spike_alerts.jsonl \
      --triage-output data/baseline/spike_triage.csv \
      --assignments-log logs/baseline_spike_team_assignments.jsonl
  - Treatment spike generation and routing:
    python scripts/integrations/gen_alerts.py \
      --output data/treatment/spike_alerts.jsonl \
      --count 60 --duration-minutes 5 --seed 123 \
      --scenario spike \
      --webhook-url http://localhost:8100/webhook/alerts
  - Validate treatment spike events in 'logs/treatment_spike_events.jsonl'.

Run Workload 3 (failure scenarios):
  - Start mock services with failure injection flags:
    python scripts/integrations/mock_chat_service.py --port 8101 --simulate-downtime 180
    python scripts/integrations/mock_ticketing_service.py --port 8102 --error-rate 0.2
    python scripts/integrations/integration_service.py --port 8100 --chat-url http://localhost:8101/chat/post_message --ticket-url http://localhost:8102/tickets
  - Generate alerts including malformed payloads:
    python scripts/integrations/gen_alerts.py \
      --output data/treatment/failure_alerts.jsonl \
      --count 40 --duration-minutes 10 --seed 777 \
      --inject-malformed 0.1 \
      --webhook-url http://localhost:8100/webhook/alerts
  - For baseline comparison, re-run with failure behaviors encoded in baseline scripts and no webhooks.

Compute metrics using the analysis notebook or script:
  - Open 'notebooks/ch11_integration_experiment_analysis.ipynb' in Jupyter, or run:
    python scripts/integrations/compute_metrics.py \
      --baseline-logs logs/baseline_tickets.jsonl logs/baseline_chat.jsonl \
      --treatment-logs logs/treatment_events.jsonl \
      --output reports/ch11_integration_metrics.json
  - The analysis will parse logs according to the evidence_schema, compute all defined metrics per workload, and write a summary JSON report.

Review results in business-friendly terms:
  - Open the generated report (e.g., 'reports/ch11_integration_metrics.json') and compare baseline vs. treatment for key metrics such as latency, coverage, routing accuracy, and unrecovered failures.
  - Use the chapter’s leadership checklist and discussion prompts to interpret what these results imply for your own organization’s integration priorities, vendor requirements, and technical debt strategies.

evidence_schema.description: Canonical schemas for logs and metric outputs produced by the integration experiments, enabling consistent analysis and interpretation.

fields.alert_id: string, unique identifier for the alert; used as a primary correlation key.
fields.timestamp_detected: string, ISO 8601 UTC timestamp when the synthetic monitoring system detected the alert.
fields.source_channel: string, channel where the signal originated (e.g., 'twitter', 'tiktok', 'news', 'internal_tipline').
fields.scenario_tag: string, optional tag describing the scenario (e.g., 'deepfake_executive_video').
fields.suspected_attack_type: string, description or category such as 'deepfake_video', 'synthetic_reviews', 'fabricated_safety_incident'.
fields.severity_score: number, e.g., 1–5 ordinal scale, higher means higher priority.
fields.confidence_score: number, 0.0–1.0, confidence in the alert’s correctness.
fields.impacted_asset: string, optional, name or identifier of the brand, product, executive, or function affected.
fields.summary_text: string, short textual description of the alert.
fields.url: string, optional, reference link to the content when applicable.
fields.raw_payload: object, optional, full raw JSON payload as received or generated.
fields.experiment_run_id: string, identifier for the experiment run instance.
fields.workload_name: string, one of the defined workloads (e.g., 'workload-1-single-stream-medium-volume').

fields.chat_event_id: string, unique identifier for the chat event.
fields.timestamp_posted: string, ISO 8601 UTC timestamp when the message was posted to chat.
fields.channel_name: string, name of the (mock) chat channel (e.g., 'comms_incidents', 'security_incidents').
fields.message_text: string, message body or summary posted.
fields.owning_team: string, which team this channel is mapped to (e.g., 'comms', 'legal', 'security').
fields.experiment_run_id: string, identifier for the experiment run instance.
fields.workload_name: string, workload under which this event occurred.
fields.delivery_status: string, 'success' or 'failure', indicates whether posting succeeded.
fields.error_detail: string, optional, error message if delivery_status == 'failure'.

fields.ticket_id: string, unique identifier for the ticket/incident.
fields.timestamp_created: string, ISO 8601 UTC timestamp when the initial ticket was created.
fields.timestamp_updated: string, optional, last updated timestamp if applicable.
fields.priority: string, mapped from severity or business rules (e.g., 'P1', 'P2', 'P3').
fields.summary: string, summary or title of the incident.
fields.experiment_run_id: string, identifier for the experiment run instance.
fields.workload_name: string, workload under which this ticket was created.

fields.timestamp: string, ISO 8601 UTC timestamp when the error was recorded.
fields.alert_id: string, optional, correlation to alert_event.alert_id if applicable.
fields.retry_count: integer, number of retries attempted (if any).
fields.recovered: boolean, whether the system ultimately succeeded in processing after the error.
fields.experiment_run_id: string, identifier for the experiment run instance.
string, identifier for the experiment run instance, grouping all results.
fields.workload_name: string, workload for which these metrics were computed.
fields.end_to_end_alert_to_ticket_latency_media: number, median latency from detection to ticket creation in seconds.
fields.end_to_end_alert_to_chat_latency_median_: number, median latency from detection to chat posting in seconds.
fields.alert_routing_coverage: number, fraction of alerts meeting routing criteria that resulted in at least one ticket and/or chat event.
fields.routing_accuracy: number, fraction of routed alerts whose owning_team matches the ground-truth mapping.
fields.operator_touch_points_per_100_alerts: number, estimated manual steps normalized per 100 alerts.
fields.unrecovered_delivery_failures: integer, count of alerts not successfully routed after retries.
fields.error_detection_rate: number, fraction of malformed alerts that were detected and logged as errors.
fields.configuration_lines: integer, count of non-comment, non-blank lines in configuration files relevant to routing.
fields.routing_rule_count: integer, number of distinct routing rules defined.
fields.notes: string, optional, free-text annotations or caveats about the run (e.g., anomalies, deviations from standard setup).
